What a Fictional Robot Can Teach Us About Care

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.
  • Sources indicate that the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie.
  • In a recent development, but when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.

Sources indicate that the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie. Josie Joy.

In a recent development, but when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie. The name was too soft, too ethereal for such a sentient, wide-awake, bird-like baby. I knew that I had to find a new name. Who are you? I whispered into the swirls of her astoundingly warm, circulated, and singularly perfect ear. I couldn’t wait to get to know her.

In another story, a girl named Josie is dying. In Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, Josie has an unknown illness and a prognosis that haunts the pages. Her life exists in the shadow of her sister, Sal, who has already died of the same unarticulated illness, likely caused by an elective genetic alteration procedure known as “lifting.”.

Recent findings suggest that in Josie’s world, being lifted is the upcoming social currency; those who are lifted are expected to have greater access to both intellectual and economic success. The procedure does not, however, come without risk. When we meet Josie’s mother, she is tasked with the impossible: coping with the impending death of her only remaining child. A death likely resulting from a choice she made as a parent. The ultimate consequence.

Klara is a robot purchased by Josie’s mom to be her companion, in part (it is implied) to assuage the guilt she feels. I first read Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun shortly after its debut. Despite being disturbed by some aspects of the dystopian world depicted within, my memory of the novel was poignant. I recalled Klara with particular affection.

Now, the distance between Ishiguro’s dystopian world and our current reality is rapidly collapsing. With the much anticipated film adaptation set to be released this Friday, October 23, and the sudden ubiquity of artificial intelligence in our day-to-day lives, Klara and the Sun is now repositioned as a mirror. If we look closely enough, we might discern what remains uniquely human during this moment of profound technological and social change.

We are introduced to Klara, the story’s narrator, when Josie’s mom takes her to find an artificial friend, or AF for short. In the novel, AFs confer social standing, but also offer practical assistance—tutoring, companionship, monitoring an ailing child—not unlike the benefits purported by artificial intelligence companies today.

Klara has been patiently waiting, alongside several other AFs, to be chosen. Josie’s mother is the final decider. In a foreboding scene, Josie’s mother commands Klara to reenact Josie’s gait—a test, of sorts—before agreeing to purchase her. It’s the precision of Klara’s mimicry that convinces “the Mother” (as she’s called in the novel) that Klara is the right model for Josie.

In a recent development, all of this, we learn through Klara. Ishiguro’s choice to position the reader within Klara’s perspective allows us to bypass the quagmire question of whether or not Klara is conscious and instead project our own consciousness onto her. In doing so, we view the human world through her sometimes malfunctioning robot eyes, as she nonjudgmentally conveys the complexities of the very flawed and sometimes desperate human behaviors she seeks to understand. In one particularly moving scene, Klara witnesses the vulnerability of caring for another human being:.

In a recent development, I saw before me, on the near edge of the bed, a large shifting shape, made additionally complex by the patches of blackness and moonlight moving over its surface. I realized the shape was the Mother and Josie embracing. . . . As well as their limbs, their hair had become mingled, and then their shape began gently to rock, in a way not unlike when their goodbyes became extended.

Sources indicate that “Don’t want to die, Mom. I don’t want that.”.

“It’s okay. Okay.” The Mother’s voice was soft, at just the same level mine had been.

In a recent development, prior to this moment, Klara—steadfast and ever-available—had offered her presence to comfort Josie. Yet, despite their far more complicated and at times strained relationship, it is the Mother that Josie calls for.

When I first became a parent, I confided to a friend that when my not-Josie was born, I felt like a newly introduced sun had burst into my solar system, and I was now orbiting around her. I couldn’t quite articulate the “before,” in my metaphor. I didn’t feel like I was previously my own sun, nor did I feel like I was a planet untethered to others. But there was something distinctly different when she arrived, a whole new consciousness, a space and force and awareness created within me. Her pull was intoxicating, undeniable, sometimes terrifying, and my awareness and attention seemed to expand overnight to now include not only my own experiences, but also to track, perceive, anticipate, and accommodate her own.

Industry observers note that if Klara had turned to psychological theory and research about the complexity of parent-child bonds, she would have found a great deal of it. Consider Winnicott’s “good-enough mother” or research indicating that parents and infants are rarely, if ever, perfectly attuned, and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the navigation of the ruptures and repairs themselves reinforce attachment. It has become increasingly clear through evolving applications of experiments such as Edward Tronick’s now famous “still-face” experiment that the imperfect dance between caregiver and child lays the groundwork for resilience and emotional regulation.

In The Philosophical Baby, developmental psychologist and philosopher Alison Gopnik states, “It’s not so much that we care for children because we love them, as that we love them because we care for them.”.

We love them because we care for them.

Beyond Gopnik’s own research, there is an abundance of data to back this up. Studies I have long been familiar with, such as those demonstrating that in same-sex, non-carrying male couples, fathers who act as primary parents show changes in similar brain regions to women who carried their pregnancies and go on to parent their children. Yet, there was something profound about the simplicity of Gopnik’s statement, about love being something we cultivate within ourselves and, more precisely, about care being the means through which we build love, not merely a necessary byproduct.

According to recent reports, in a separate interview, Gopnik jokes that spending time with a three-year-old gives you a small taste of sainthood. Not in the sense that the demands are so extreme that you inherently become a saint (though there is a real argument to be made here for any parent who weathers the storm of a parking lot tantrum), but in the actual felt-sense of the divine, the experience of feeling so acutely and utterly in love with this being, so in awe of their singularity, their specialness, their openness to experience, their brilliance.

Sources indicate that gopnik continues on, teasing, about our tendency to claim the uniqueness of our three-year-old, in her case her grandchild, but gently affirms the truth beneath: that there is something numinous, universal, pure within all three-year-olds, a near-magical vitality that we sometimes make contact with when we intimately care for one. Something primal, or perhaps primary, is awoken when we re-experience the world through the eyes of a three-year-old.

It has been revealed that my not-Josie is now three. In many ways she is more unknowable, separate, than she was when she was a newborn, so physically attached and dependent on me. Now, she has her own relationships—with teachers, classmates, family members—that are entirely her own. And yet, she occupies and orients so much of me, continually changing my experience of the world, my access to play, to awe, to unadulterated, intoxicating adoration.

This past summer, I was sitting by a lake, relaxed but hawk-eyed as I watched my not-Josie from the shore. I felt a familiar presence by my side, the barely-perceptible shadow in my peripheral vision of a small body sitting down, and soon thereafter, the unselfconscious weight of a small hand on my leg. I looked down to see a head covered in feathery blonde hair, not the dark, curly brown of my own child.

It has been revealed that the wispy tufts belonged to another small child who had clearly mistaken me for her mother. In that brief moment before she looked up, before we both acknowledged our separateness, I felt overcome with the awareness—as though received through the touch of her hand on my leg—that her mother loved her in the way that I love my child, and that, despite how unbelievably special my not-Josie is, my love for her is not. It is precious, but also universal.

According to recent reports, intellectually, of course, this is not a profound realization. Emotionally touching into it is, on the other hand, equally as brutal as it is beautiful. Next to this small child, healthy and safe, I felt her preciousness, but also that of all the children flooding my news feed every day who are not healthy and safe, and whose parents must live with this love and that devastation.

On the back cover, Klara and the Sun is described as a story about love, which it undeniably is. But I think it’s perhaps more fundamentally about care.

Care is arguably more tangible than love, but also more complex, friction-prone, messy. It’s the gaps, the mistakes, the harms, the repairs, the precarity, the forgiving, that make care so deeply painful and so deeply nourishing. Nourishing enough to sustain the vulnerability of love.

In a recent development, it is care that drives Josie’s mother to have her “lifted” in an age-old attempt of desperation to give her child what she perceives as the best chance at a full life in a rapidly reorganizing world. It is care that sends the Mother down the path of trying to find a way to have Klara “continue” Josie’s life, even though she has already tried and failed to recreate her first child’s consciousness in an artificial intelligence through the work of an artist and scientist named Capaldi.

In a recent development, it is care that allows the Mother—despite her cold exterior—to fearlessly comfort her child as she confronts the possibility of her own death, enveloping her, rocking her, soothing her through the unimaginable. It is the Mother’s human care, not her cowardice, that makes her love true.

There is so much in Klara and the Sun that is undeniably relevant in this particular social, cultural, and technological moment, so many ways in which Ishiguro’s Josie and my not-Josie’s world are suddenly uncomfortably proximate, but it is what Klara herself affirms about humanity that is most resonant.

In a recent development, at the end of the novel, Klara reflects on what she’s learned. She did not have to become a Josie 2.0, for Josie survived. Klara is glad for this, of course, believing that it was her bargain with the Sun (which she sees as a kind of god) that saved Josie. Sitting discarded in a junk yard, Klara is increasingly convinced that the desperate blueprint to turn Josie into a digital consciousness wouldn’t have worked:.

In a recent development, mr. Capaldi believed there was nothing special inside Josie that couldn’t be continued. He told the Mother he’d searched and searched and found nothing like that. But I believe now he was searching in the wrong place. There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie. It was inside those who loved her. That’s why I think now Mr. Capaldi was wrong and I wouldn’t have succeeded.

It is what happens within us and between us when we care for another being that differentiates us as humans. In other words, it’s not so much what’s there but what’s not there—the space between the person in front of us and how we perceive, imperfectly care for, and ultimately love them—that makes us human.

According to recent reports, through Klara’s eyes, I was able to see more clearly what connects the Mother and her Josie to me and my not-Josie. It is the very fact that we can so wholeheartedly love another being, without being them, having them, solving them, knowing every bit of them. It is the fact that still, we carry them in our hearts, and somehow we are not heavier for it.

She is the founder of Heartwork Leadership Practice, where she helps people navigating transitions, such as emerging leaders, new parents, and career changers, develop the self-awareness and self-regard to lead from a place of purpose.

#68998. Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger

Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that stress does more than influence how we feel.
  • Researchers at Yale University have now uncovered key clues.
  • "We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," noted corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that stress does more than influence how we feel. It can also change what we remember, particularly when an experience is emotionally intense or personally meaningful. Scientists have long known that cortisol, a hormone released during stressful situations, can strengthen emotional memories. What has been less clear is exactly how this happens inside the brain.

Researchers at Yale University have now uncovered key clues. Their study reveals that cortisol strengthens emotional memories by changing how brain networks involved in emotion and memory function and communicate with one another. The findings offer a deeper understanding of why certain experiences leave such powerful impressions while others quickly fade.

"We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," noted corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

How Stress Hormones Influence Memory.

Previous research involving both humans and rodents has shown that stress and cortisol can improve memory for emotional events. Scientists also know that certain brain regions, including the amygdala, play an essential role in this process. The amygdala is particularly important for processing emotions and identifying experiences that may be significant.

However, understanding precisely how cortisol strengthens memories has been challenging. Many brain regions participate in several mental functions, making it difficult to determine whether the hormone is influencing emotional responses, memory formation, or both.

"Forming memories for emotional experiences involves different processes in the brain: first, perceiving an experience as emotional or intense, and second, encoding that experience into long-term memory," remarked Goldfarb, who is also a member of Yale's Wu Tsai Institute, an interdisciplinary research initiative that explores cognition.

The researchers wanted to examine these processes separately to determine how cortisol affects the brain's ability to recognize emotional significance and preserve an experience as a lasting memory.

Watching the Brain Form Emotional Memories.

According to recent reports, to investigate, the Yale team conducted an experiment in which participants took a pill containing either hydrocortisone, a form of cortisol, or an inactive placebo. They then viewed a series of pictures while undergoing functional MRI (fMRI) scanning.

This imaging technique measures changes in blood flow and oxygen levels associated with brain activity, allowing researchers to identify which areas of the brain are more active during different tasks.

It has been revealed that as participants examined the pictures, they reported their emotional reactions to each image. The following day, researchers tested how well they remembered what they had seen.

Each person completed the experiment twice, once after receiving hydrocortisone and once after receiving the placebo. The study used a double blind design, meaning neither the participants nor the experimenter knew which substance had been administered during a particular session.

This approach allowed the scientists to compare how the same person's brain responded with and without the additional cortisol.

A Five-Second Look at Brain Network Activity.

One of the study's most important advances came from the way researchers analyzed the brain scans.

Industry observers note that scientists often study a measurement called functional connectivity, which describes how closely activity in different parts of the brain fluctuates together. When two regions show synchronized patterns of activity, it can indicate that they are participating in related processes.

Sources indicate that traditionally, examining these relationships requires several minutes of brain imaging data. The Yale team instead analyzed functional connectivity during individual trials lasting only around five seconds.

Using these brief snapshots, the researchers tested whether patterns of brain activity could predict two different outcomes: how emotionally intense participants found a picture and whether they would remember that picture the following day.

It has been revealed that the approach worked for both. By identifying patterns associated with emotional intensity and memory formation separately, the scientists were able to examine how cortisol influenced each network and the interactions between them.

This gave the researchers a more detailed picture of the changing brain activity associated with emotional memory formation.

Cortisol Changes How Brain Networks Work Together.

The results revealed two major effects.

First, cortisol improved participants' ability to remember emotionally significant experiences, confirming what earlier research had suggested.

Second, and more importantly, the hormone strengthened emotional memory through distinct changes in the brain networks responsible for processing emotion and forming memories.

In a recent development, in networks associated with emotion, cortisol produced more consistent patterns of activity and increased their engagement. This suggests that the hormone helped the brain respond more strongly and reliably to the emotional significance of an experience.

In memory networks, cortisol had a different effect. It made their activity patterns more specialized for emotional information, suggesting that the brain was adjusting how it encoded emotionally meaningful experiences.

According to recent reports, the hormone also increased coordination between the networks involved in emotion and memory. In other words, cortisol appeared to help these different brain systems work together more effectively when processing experiences that carried emotional weight.

Together, these findings suggest that stress strengthens emotional memories through several interacting brain mechanisms rather than through a single region or process.

Why Emotional Experiences Can Be So Memorable.

Industry observers note that the results help explain why stress does not necessarily improve memory for everything. Instead, its benefits appear to be selective, making experiences that feel particularly intense or meaningful more likely to be remembered.

The researchers believe this reflects the brain's ability to adapt to stressful situations by prioritizing information that may be notable.

"Stress responses are fundamentally adaptive and can help you form strong memories -- but this is specific to experiences that you find to be emotionally intense or meaningful," Goldfarb mentioned. "This is in part related to your brain increasing engagement of networks that track emotional intensity. So, if you are stressed out and trying to learn something latest, it might help to think about exciting elements or strong feelings connected to what you are learning.".

The findings also point to a potentially useful insight about learning. Connecting information to something exciting, personally vital, or emotionally engaging could make it easier to remember, particularly during stressful situations.

Rather than simply disrupting memory, stress can sometimes help the brain identify which experiences deserve special attention and strengthen the networks involved in preserving them.

Other Yale researchers involved in the study include Rajita Sinha, the Foundations Fund Endowed Professor in Psychiatry and professor in the Child Study Center and of neuroscience at Yale School of Medicine (YSM), and Todd Constable, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson Professor of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging and professor of neurosurgery at YSM.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health.

Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next.

Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness. The findings, published in the journal Nature, challenge traditional assumptions about the relationship between consciousness and thinking. They could also provide upcoming insights into how the brain processes memories and language, potentially leading to advances in technologies that help people communicate after neurological injuries.

Recent findings suggest that "Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," noted Dr. Sameer Sheth, professor and Cullen Foundation Endowed chair of neurosurgery and a McNair Scholar at Baylor. "Even when patients are fully anesthetized, their brains continue to analyze the world around them.".

Recording Brain Activity During General Anesthesia.

To investigate what happens inside the unconscious brain, Sheth, who is also a neurosurgeon at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center, and his colleagues studied patients undergoing epilepsy surgery while under general anesthesia.

These procedures offered an unusual opportunity to examine the hippocampus, a brain structure deeply involved in learning and memory. Located within the brain's temporal lobe, the hippocampus helps organize information and plays an crucial role in forming newly introduced memories.

It has been revealed that the researchers used advanced recording devices called Neuropixels probes to monitor electrical signals from hundreds of individual neurons in the hippocampus. These tiny probes can detect activity from many nerve cells simultaneously, providing a detailed picture of how groups of neurons respond to information.

Recent findings suggest that according to the researchers, this technology had not previously been used to investigate this particular brain region in this way. It allowed the team to examine how the hippocampus responds to sounds and language while patients are unconscious and unable to report what they experience.

The first experiment involved playing a series of repeating tones, occasionally interrupted by a sound that differed from the others.

According to recent reports, although the patients were under anesthesia, neurons in their hippocampus responded differently to the unexpected sounds. Even more surprisingly, the brain cells became better at distinguishing these unusual tones as the experiment continued.

This improvement suggested that the hippocampus was showing signs of neural plasticity, the brain's ability to change its responses through experience. In other words, some of the basic processes associated with learning appeared to remain active even without conscious awareness.

The Unconscious Brain Can Process Language and Predict Words.

The researchers then tested whether the unconscious brain could handle something more complicated than simple sounds.

They played short stories to the anesthetized patients while continuing to record activity from neurons in the hippocampus.

According to recent reports, the results revealed a surprising level of language processing. Distinct patterns of neural activity contained information about different categories of words, including nouns, verbs, and adjectives. This suggested that the hippocampus was responding to meaningful features of language rather than simply detecting that sounds were occurring.

But the most intriguing discovery went a step further.

In a recent development, the researchers found that neural activity also carried information that could be used to predict upcoming words in a sentence. Even though the patients were unconscious, their brains appeared to anticipate how the language unfolding around them might continue.

"The brain appears to anticipate what comes next in a story, even without conscious awareness," stated Sheth, who is also Director of The Gordon and Mary Cain Pediatric Neurology Research Foundation Laboratories within the Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's Hospital.

This ability is related to a process known as predictive coding. Rather than passively receiving information, the brain continually uses patterns and previous experience to anticipate what might happen next. When listening to someone speak, for example, the brain can use the words already heard to form expectations about what is likely to follow.

It has been revealed that scientists have typically studied this kind of sophisticated prediction in people who are awake and paying attention. Finding evidence of it during general anesthesia suggests that at least some of the underlying neural processes can operate independently of conscious awareness.

Recent findings suggest that "This kind of predictive coding is something we associate with being awake and attentive, yet it's happening here in an unconscious state," said Dr. Benjamin Hayden, professor of neurosurgery at Baylor.

What Does This Discovery Mean for Consciousness?

The findings raise notable questions about what consciousness actually contributes to the brain's ability to process information.

Sources indicate that consciousness is generally associated with subjective awareness, including the experience of hearing, thinking, and understanding the world around us. Yet the study suggests that some neural processes involved in interpreting language and predicting future information can continue even when that awareness is absent.

Recent findings suggest that this does not necessarily mean that the anesthetized patients consciously understood the stories being played to them. Instead, it indicates that the brain can carry out surprisingly complex aspects of language processing without a person being aware of doing so.

The distinction could help researchers better understand how consciousness emerges.

One possibility is that awareness depends not simply on whether individual brain regions remain active, but on how information is coordinated and shared across larger networks of brain regions.

Under this view, a structure such as the hippocampus might continue analyzing information even when the broader communication between brain regions needed for conscious experience is disrupted.

A Surprising Connection Between the Brain and Artificial Intelligence.

The discovery also highlights an intriguing similarity between human brain activity and artificial intelligence (AI).

Large language models, the technology behind many modern AI chatbots, generate text by using patterns learned from enormous amounts of language data to predict what should come next.

The researchers observed a related predictive ability in the hippocampus, where neural signals reflected information about upcoming words even during unconsciousness.

Although biological brains and AI models operate in fundamentally different ways, both can use patterns in language to anticipate future information. Studying these similarities may help scientists better understand how prediction works in natural and artificial systems.

The findings could also have practical implications for brain-computer interfaces, which use signals recorded from the brain to communicate with external devices.

One potential application involves speech prosthetics, technologies designed to help people communicate when injuries or neurological conditions have impaired their ability to speak.

If scientists can reliably identify meaningful language signals in the brain, those signals might eventually be used to support communication technologies for patients who have lost speech abilities.

It has been revealed that "Can we use these signals to deploy and run a speech prosthetic for some of the parts of the brain that are damaged by stroke or injury? These are questions that we can now consider in relation to this part of the brain," remarked Dr. Vigi Katlowitz, first author and a neurosurgery resident with Baylor.

Scientists Are Rethinking the Limits of the Unconscious Brain.

Despite the striking results, the researchers emphasize that several questions remain unanswered.

The experiments were conducted under one particular type of general anesthesia, so the findings cannot automatically be extended to other anesthetic methods or states of unconsciousness.

It is also unclear whether similar language processing occurs during sleep or coma, two conditions that differ significantly from medically induced unconsciousness.

Recent findings suggest that another key limitation is that the researchers focused on the hippocampus. Further studies will be needed to determine whether comparable abilities persist in other brain regions and how these areas interact when consciousness is absent.

Nevertheless, the results provide compelling evidence that unconsciousness does not necessarily mean the brain has stopped performing sophisticated information processing.

Instead, the brain may continue analyzing patterns, responding to unexpected events, and anticipating language even when a person has no conscious awareness of the surrounding world.

Sources indicate that "This work pushes us to rethink what it means to be conscious," mentioned Sheth. "The brain is doing much more behind the scenes than we fully understand.".

Ten TV Series That Highlight the Best in Humanity: 2026

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, every year, we invite staff and regular contributors to nominate TV series for Greater Goodies, the awards we give to stories that exemplify or illustrate kindness, community, empathy, and more keys to well-being.
  • In a recent development, name the last show you’ve seen that features a hero over the age of 60.
  • According to recent reports, with a star-studded lead cast, all 70 or older, we follow Sam Cooper’s (Alfred Molina) experience as he reluctantly moves into a senior living community in New Mexico after the death of his wife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every year, we invite staff and regular contributors to nominate TV series for Greater Goodies, the awards we give to stories that exemplify or illustrate kindness, community, empathy, and more keys to well-being. Here’s what we came up with this year: The Boroughs, Death by Lightning, Envidiosa, The Hawk, Heated Rivalry, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, Lucky, Murderbot, Pluribus, and Shrinking.

In a recent development, name the last show you’ve seen that features a hero over the age of 60. Drawing a blank? It’s not your fault—the media’s modus operandi is to equate heroism with youthfulness. Netflix’s The Boroughs flips this stereotype on its head.

According to recent reports, with a star-studded lead cast, all 70 or older, we follow Sam Cooper’s (Alfred Molina) experience as he reluctantly moves into a senior living community in New Mexico after the death of his wife. But a series of strange events suggests that this is no ordinary retirement community.

According to recent reports, as Sam navigates grief, newly introduced friendships, and a new identity, he joins forces with his neighbors to solve and resolve the community mystery. Overcoming obstacles like age discrimination and self-doubts, the group peels back the layers of the strange occurrences. At the root of the mystery is a societal fear of aging.

According to recent reports, the show highlights what researcher Margie Lachman calls “crystallized intelligence”: the culmination of life experience, memory, and know-how. In The Boroughs, that turns out to be just as heroic as super human strength or the ability to fly. — Shanna B. Tiayon.

History has already told us how Death by Lightning ends: Charles Guiteau will assassinate President James Garfield in 1881. But why? That’s one of the questions explored by the series, and it finds motivation in a sense of purpose–how purpose forms and how people come to cross-purposes.

According to recent reports, garfield (Michael Shannon) is principled and drawn reluctantly into a presidential contest he entered to nominate someone else. Guiteau (Matthew Macfadyen), meanwhile, is disturbingly sympathetic: charming, articulate, and desperate to do something meaningful with his life. Despite failed ventures, including a stint at the Oneida free-love commune, he remains convinced greatness awaits him. Believing his campaigning secured Garfield’s victory, he expects a government position to confirm his worth.

In a recent development, as their stories converge, Garfield finds purpose in his presidency: fighting corruption while supporting education and equal opportunity. Guiteau pursues a reward he feels he deserves, an entitlement that leads to tragedy.

In these ways, Garfield and Guiteau offer sharply contrasting answers to what makes a life meaningful, and watching their stories unfold side by side, we see how differently the desire to matter can play out.

In a recent development, who you really ought to be watching closely is Garfield’s Vice President, Chester A. Arthur (Nick Offerman). A comfortable beneficiary of the political machine, he becomes an unlikely source of hope as the story goes on. Offerman makes him funny, flawed, and increasingly affecting as the demands of office begin to collide with old loyalties.

Sources indicate that in a political landscape that can leave us cynical–in both the 19th century and the 21st–the series makes room for something more hopeful: the possibility that even an unlikely person can rise to the occasion, if they know why they need to rise. – Aurelia Santos.

When almost-40-year-old Vicky (Griselda Siciliani) breaks up with her long-term boyfriend, she is driven to embark upon a journey of self-discovery.

At first, Vicky is just looking for a replacement for her boyfriend—but the problem is that her compulsive comparisons with other women sabotage attempts to connect with other people. (Indeed, the name of this Argentinian show, Envidiosa, means “envious.”) Vicky is self-absorbed and yet at the same time she doesn’t have a strong sense of her own self.

It has been revealed that we see this vividly in her hilarious sessions with her therapist. When, for example, she goes on an envious rant about a friend’s milestone, she is forced to confront the quiet, uncomfortable realization that she never once asked how her friend actually felt. In short, Vicky is not a polished role model—and over the course of four seasons, we see her empathy grow through the painful process of unlearning self-centeredness.

It has been revealed that personally, I see Envidiosa as an opportunity to question how we show up for others’ joys and struggles, and I take it as an invitation to reflect: How can I empathize with the ups and downs of those around me? Envidiosa is a funny and at times embarrassingly relatable story about trying to become a more empathic human being and friend. — Criss Cuervo.

In The Hawk, washed-up professional golfer Lonnie “The Hawk” Hawkins (Will Ferrell) has made a miracle comeback into the PGA tour—this time around, facing a tough competitor in his son, Lance (Jimmy Tatro).

Industry observers note that it’s a screwball comedy, full of dirty jokes and a rapid-fire rapport between Lonnie and his not-quite-ex-wife, Stacy (Molly Shannon). A makeshift-caddy he “picked up at Walmart” (while chatting up the parking lot, from his camper van) adds to the fun, serving up an unlikely duo that seem happy just to be alive.

Recent findings suggest that even when he’s pretty down and out, Lonnie is looking on the bright side of things. Everything is done with gusto—he chats up the golf ball before each swing, he devours plates of Buffalo Wild Wings, he plays mini golf with his son and makes it a full-on competition.

In a recent development, “Son, never play golf angry,” he tells Lance. For Lonnie, life is all about golf—and golf is all about fun. Why spend all your time on something if you aren’t doing it for the joy of it?

It has been revealed that I especially love Lonnie’s adoration for his estranged wife, a firecracker in her own right. In episode four, when the Hawk crashes his son’s engagement party–yes, you read that right–and then attempts a getaway with his caddie in the van, Stacy hurls the cake at them, along with a string of expletives.

It has been revealed that it doesn’t even faze him. “You gotta love the passion!” Lonnie gushes. “That is one hot tamale!” — Hope Reese.

Heated Rivalry follows stick-crossed lovers Shane and Ilya as they figure out how to be intimate within the highly competitive, homophobic environment of professional hockey.

At first, Shane and Ilya swap fluids more readily than emotions. But over the course of six episodes, the two learn to love across gaps in culture, language, and experience. In one pivotal scene, Shane invites Ilya to speak vulnerably about family dynamics in Ilya’s native Russian—despite not understanding a word of it.

That works because Shane does not focus attention on himself. Instead, he stays present on the phone, serving as a witness to Ilya’s visceral emotions. Their connection lies in felt care, in hearing the texture of another’s heartbreak.

It has been revealed that in similar fashion, Ilya grounds Shane in stressful encounters. He supports Shane through panic without wallowing in his lover’s fear and entices Shane to relish pleasures outside of straight standards. As a couple, they help each other explore complex parts of themselves. We see a similar process unfold in another couple in the show, as they learn to respect each other’s different needs.

Industry observers note that people might tune into Heated Rivalry for locker room towel drops and HBO’s glossy cinematography. They should stay to see a couple learn to love each other’s differences. The show exemplifies how bridging differences, at its best, means supporting others to more fully encounter themselves, and how in the process our relationships can grow.

Recent findings suggest that with plenty of additional homoerotic stick-and-ball games to pull on from the novels of Rachel Reid, the next season of Heated Rivalry is expected to air on HBO Max and Canada’s Crave in Spring 2027. — Luke Brown.

Industry observers note that the monstrously successful HBO series Game of Thrones famously tossed out a lot of good-and-evil fantasy tropes to tell a morally complicated story of how power corrupts even the best people. A prequel called House of the Dragon shares that worldview.

That’s why a new prequel called A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms came as something of a surprise to fans. Unlike the other two series, this is not a story about a struggle for power. Instead, it focuses on a rather naive, not-too-bright “hedge knight” named Duncan (Peter Claffey) seeking to be hired by whatever lord will take him. Though Duncan is taller and stronger than most, he’s touchingly childlike as he tries to find his place in the merry old kingdoms of Westeros.

In a recent development, the first two episodes are funny and charming, as Duncan acquires a squire in the form of a little bald boy going by the name Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell), and fumblingly tries to enter a jousting tournament. And then Duncan finds himself on a collision course with the great and powerful of Westeros. When violence finally comes, there’s nothing casual about it. We feel the force of every blow, the tragedy of every death, and the erosion of Duncan’s innocence.

Industry observers note that I’m giving A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms the award for integrity, but I can’t tell you why without spoiling the ending. Let’s just say that the series turns out to be the story of how one simple young man discovers what is most important to him—and finds the courage to stick to that path even in the face of isolation, temptations, and threats. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

How do you exit a life you were born into?

Recent findings suggest that that’s the question behind Lucky, starring Anya Taylor-Joy. Lucky was raised by her con-artist father and taught the “family business” from a young age—but when we meet her, she navigating internal conflict with the life she’s been told to live and the life she wants for herself.

Sources indicate that her desire to quit is complicated by her marriage to Cary, the son of a ruthless mob leader, who was also socialized into a life of crime. The couple plan one final con as their exit strategy, but it goes terribly wrong. Lucky sets out to resolve the botched plan, reconcile her marriage, and protect both her life and her father’s.

Sources indicate that her intelligence is put to the test as she puts the pieces together, connects the dots, and outsmarts her rivals. In the process she discovers her own virtue—and that the intelligence which made her a successful con artist can also set her free.

Sources indicate that through the course of the series, she realizes that she does not have to pay for the sins of her father. Having never been given the opportunity for self-determination, she makes peace in the best way she knows how and chooses a new path. — Shanna B. Tiayon.

It has been revealed that the Murderbot Diaries are a series of science-fiction novellas by Martha Wells, about a genderless, robotic soldier who manages to achieve free will. Since discovery will result in deactivation and since it doesn’t like humans very much anyway, Murderbot conceals its freedom of mind and consumes a lot of human-made entertainment inside its own head, even as it externally follows every order given to it by the evil corporation that owns it. Murderbot even has a favorite TV show: the Star-Trek-like Rise and Fall of Sanctuary Moon.

Recent findings suggest that as a result of this isolation, the novellas are built almost entirely around its memorable inner monologues, with a voice that is by turns snarky, vulnerable, cold-blooded, disgusted, and puzzled. One of the things that makes these books distinctive is that Murderbot is not Pinocchio—it has no wish to become a “real boy.” It doesn’t want a gender, or the same feelings and drives as people. It just wants to be itself—and to have that difference respected.

While the Apple TV show based on the books is not quite that original or interesting, Murderbot retains its focus on finding the balance between belonging and difference. When we meet Murderbot (Alexander Skarsgård), he’s been hired to protect a group of polyamorous hippie scientists who hail from a utopian colony that exists independently of the corporations that rule the rest of the galaxy.

It has been revealed that they are Murderbot’s first encounter with humans not shaped by dehumanizing hyper-capitalistic values, and they observe Murderbot in a way the corporate humans cannot. Over the course of the first season, they begin to realize that there is more to Murderbot than meets the eye, and they learn to see and appreciate Murderbot on its own terms. But what’s crucial is not that they perceive the humanity in the not-human Murderbot—it’s that Murderbot sees the humanity (and the goodness) in them.

It has been revealed that in time, it becomes an accepted part of their society, without becoming more like them. Even so, the first season concludes on a tough-minded, melancholy note, as Murderbot itself can’t quite feel like it belongs. Will it someday find a place among these crunchy idealists? Stay tuned: The second season is coming in 2027. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

Have you ever been among people but you didn’t feel part of the crowd? Like they were in on a joke that you just couldn’t get?

According to recent reports, welcome to Carol Sturka’s world. The science-fiction premise of Pluribus is that an alien virus transforms humanity into one massive happy hive mind—everyone except Carol and 13 other people who seem to have immunity.

Recent findings suggest that even among those remaining individuals, though, Carol stands out as a malcontent. We sense that she’s been a fish out of water for her whole life.

It has been revealed that indeed, not every viewer will find Carol relatable or likable. When we first meet her, she’s at a bookstore event promoting her highly successful romantasy series. With her fans, she’s charming, funny, and kind. When she gets into a limo after a big sendoff by readers, the driver asks if she’s famous.

“That depends,” Carol replies. “Are you a big fan of mindless crap?”.

In short, Carol hates herself, her work, and her readers. And as we discover, her personality is snarky, uptight, stubborn, and uncompromising. When the virus hits, it’s an apocalyptic event, but Carol doesn’t change one bit—and her traits become both a blessing and a curse. The whole world wants to be kind to her, but Carol can’t accept kindness. That drives her to fight back. And that’s what ultimately makes her the hero of the story.

In the end, Pluribus is a very Greater Good thought experiment. It takes prosociality to its limits and finds that a total togetherness, empathy, and cooperation to the exclusion of selfishness, crankiness, and boundaries is a self-destructive dystopia, not a utopia. The show seems to argue that humanity needs difficult people like Carol to survive, and so invites us to appreciate what the Carols of the world have to offer. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

In Shrinking, talking and listening are the name of the game. Jimmy (Jason Segel) is a widowed psychotherapist who helps patients navigate anxiety, OCD, PTSD, and other ailments as he himself is floundering.

But he’s not alone. His teenage daughter, overbearing-but-lovable neighbors, and coworker-friends (with Harrison Ford as the curmudgeonly head of the practice) are all there to help him when his life goes off the rails after his wife was killed by a drunk driver.

Recent findings suggest that in its three-season run, the series is heavy-handed with its use of therapy-speak among the whole gang, whether between therapist-to-patient, therapist-to-daughter, or therapist-to-therapist. Characters “feel seen.” More times than I can count, they tell each other “I hear you.” We witness, in detail, exchanges inside the therapy office—and outside of it, in a rogue practice known as “Jimmying,” where therapy takes place at such venues as, for instance, the boxing ring.

Sources indicate that in other words, there’s a lot of “deep listening”: the practice of being present, open, and empathic with another person, in a way that goes beyond just hearing and understanding words. In his grief, Jimmy himself is not always a perfect deep listener. He tends to talk more than a typical therapist, and frequently injects himself into the discussion. Shrinking isn’t about perfection—it’s about struggling to connect and growing in the process. – Hope Reese.

Luke Brown is the Bridging Differences Facilitator of the Bridging Differences program at UC Berkeley’s Greater Good Science Center and a PhD candidate in higher education at Boston College. He creates conditions for people to more deeply encounter one another and embrace interdependency, restorative relation, and shared futures.

#68995. Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain

📅 17 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1518 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain

📅 17 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A good night's sleep does much more than leave you feeling refreshed.
  • Scientists have long known that insufficient sleep can interfere with growth hormone production.
  • Now, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have uncovered the brain circuitry behind this relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A good night's sleep does much more than leave you feeling refreshed. During deep sleep, the body releases growth hormone, a powerful chemical messenger that helps build muscle, strengthen bones, and regulate fat metabolism. For teenagers, getting enough sleep is especially important because growth hormone plays a major role in reaching their full height potential.

Scientists have long known that insufficient sleep can interfere with growth hormone production. What remained unclear was exactly how the brain controls this process, particularly during non-REM sleep, the deep, restorative stage that typically dominates the earlier part of the night.

Now, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have uncovered the brain circuitry behind this relationship. In a study published in the journal Cell, the team identified the neurons that regulate growth hormone release during sleep and discovered a previously unknown feedback system that helps maintain a delicate balance between hormone levels and wakefulness.

The discovery reveals that the relationship works in both directions. Sleep stimulates growth hormone production, but growth hormone also sends signals back to the brain that influence when we wake up.

The findings could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to treating sleep disorders associated with metabolic diseases such as diabetes, as well as neurological conditions including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.

In a recent development, "People know that growth hormone release is tightly related to sleep, but only through drawing blood and checking growth hormone levels during sleep," noted study first author Xinlu Ding, a postdoctoral fellow in UC Berkeley's Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute. "We're actually directly recording neural activity in mice to see what's going on. We are providing a basic circuit to work on in the future to develop different treatments.".

Why Deep Sleep Matters for Growth and Metabolism.

It has been revealed that growth hormone is best known for its role in childhood development, but its importance extends well into adulthood. It supports the maintenance of muscle and bone, helps the body regulate how it uses stored fat, and influences blood sugar levels.

Industry observers note that when sleep is consistently disrupted, growth hormone regulation can suffer. Because this hormone helps control glucose and fat metabolism, inadequate sleep may contribute to an increased risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.

To understand how the brain coordinates these processes, the Berkeley researchers focused on a region called the hypothalamus. Located deep within the brain, this small but essential control center helps regulate hunger, body temperature, hormone production, and the daily cycle of sleeping and waking. Its basic functions have been preserved throughout mammalian evolution.

Within the hypothalamus, the researchers examined neurons that produce growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) and two distinct types of neurons that produce somatostatin.

Sources indicate that these chemical messengers have opposing functions. GHRH encourages growth hormone secretion, while somatostatin suppresses it. Together, they help control how much growth hormone enters the bloodstream, largely by regulating its release from the pituitary gland, a small hormone-producing structure at the base of the brain.

The scientists also investigated how growth hormone influences the locus coeruleus, a region in the brainstem involved in alertness, attention, thinking, and the drive to explore new or unfamiliar experiences.

Disruptions in the activity of this region have been linked to several psychiatric and neurological disorders.

Sources indicate that "Understanding the neural circuit for growth hormone release could eventually point toward new hormonal therapies to improve sleep quality or restore normal growth hormone balance," noted Daniel Silverman, a UC Berkeley postdoctoral fellow and study co-author. "There are some experimental gene therapies where you target a specific cell type. This circuit could be a novel handle to try to dial back the excitability of the locus coeruleus, which hasn't been talked about before.".

Scientists Map the Brain Circuit That Controls Growth Hormone.

The research was conducted in the laboratory of Yang Dan, a professor of neuroscience and of molecular and cell biology at UC Berkeley.

According to recent reports, to investigate how the circuitry works, the team studied mice using electrodes implanted in their brains. The scientists recorded neural activity while using light to stimulate specific neurons in the hypothalamus, allowing them to observe how different parts of the system responded.

Industry observers note that mice are particularly useful for studying sleep regulation because their sleep patterns differ significantly from those of humans. Rather than sleeping through one long stretch each night, mice typically sleep in brief episodes lasting only several minutes, scattered throughout the day and night.

This gave the researchers repeated opportunities to examine how neural activity and growth hormone regulation changed as the animals moved between sleeping and waking.

Using advanced techniques to trace connections between brain cells, the team discovered that GHRH and somatostatin behave differently depending on the stage of sleep.

During rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, the stage commonly associated with vivid dreaming, activity involving both GHRH and somatostatin increases. Although these hormones normally exert opposing effects, their coordinated activity during this stage contributes to increased growth hormone release.

Sources indicate that during non-REM sleep, the pattern changes. Somatostatin activity decreases, reducing its inhibitory influence, while GHRH activity rises moderately. This combination also promotes growth hormone secretion.

The discovery helps explain how different sleep stages can support the release of the same essential hormone through distinct patterns of brain activity.

Growth Hormone Also Helps Control When We Wake Up.

Industry observers note that perhaps the most surprising finding was that growth hormone does not simply respond to signals from the sleeping brain. It also influences the brain circuits that control wakefulness.

As growth hormone gradually builds up during sleep, it stimulates neurons in the locus coeruleus, increasing their activity and helping promote the transition toward waking.

This creates a feedback loop in which sleep encourages growth hormone release, and the resulting hormone activity helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

The researchers also identified an unexpected complication. Although greater activity in the locus coeruleus generally promotes alertness, excessive stimulation can have the opposite effect.

In an earlier study published the same year, Silverman demonstrated that when neurons in this region become overexcited, they can paradoxically promote sleepiness rather than wakefulness.

Together, these findings reveal a carefully regulated system in which the brain must balance competing signals to maintain healthy sleep and hormone activity.

Scientists describe this type of self-regulating process as homeostasis, the body's ability to maintain stable internal conditions even as its environment and physiological demands change.

"This suggests that sleep and growth hormone form a tightly balanced system: Too little sleep reduces growth hormone release, and too much growth hormone can in turn push the brain toward wakefulness," Silverman said. "Sleep drives growth hormone release, and growth hormone feeds back to regulate wakefulness, and this balance is essential for growth, repair and metabolic health.".

A Surprising Connection Between Sleep and Brain Health.

The newly identified feedback system may have implications that extend beyond physical growth and metabolism.

Because the locus coeruleus helps regulate attention, alertness, and cognitive function, growth hormone's influence on this region suggests it could also play a role in how effectively the brain functions after waking.

This raises the possibility that maintaining healthy sleep and growth hormone rhythms may support both physical recovery and mental performance.

"Growth hormone not only helps you build your muscle and bones and reduce your fat tissue, but may also have cognitive benefits, promoting your overall arousal level when you wake up," Ding stated.

By identifying the specific brain cells and signaling pathways involved, the researchers have provided a foundation for exploring therapies that target disrupted sleep and hormone regulation.

Such approaches could eventually prove useful for people with sleep disturbances related to metabolic disorders or neurological diseases. However, the experiments were conducted in mice, and additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans and whether they can be safely targeted with treatments.

In a recent development, the findings underscore a fundamental principle of sleep biology: Rest is not simply a period when the brain switches off. It is an active, carefully coordinated process in which hormones and neural circuits constantly communicate to support growth, repair, metabolism, and wakefulness.

Research Funding and Contributors.

The research was supported by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI), which supported Dan as an HHMI investigator until the year of the study's publication, and the Pivotal Life Sciences Chancellor's Chair fund.

Dan holds the Pivotal Life Sciences Chancellor's Chair in Neuroscience.

Additional co-authors include Peng Zhong, Bing Li, Chenyan Ma, Lihui Lu, Grace Jiang, Zhe Zhang, Xiaolin Huang, Xun Tu, and Zhiyu Melissa Tian of UC Berkeley, along with Fuu-Jiun Hwang and Jun Ding of Stanford University.

Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#68994. Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief

Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists at Mount Sinai have identified three crucial brain connections associated with long-term improvement in patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) for severe depression that has not responded to conventional treatments.
  • Published October 1 in the American Journal of Psychiatry, the research examined the largest group of patients assembled across multiple independent cohorts to date who had received subcallosal cingulate deep brain stimulation (SCC DBS) for treatment-resistant depression.
  • The researchers found that lasting improvements were consistently associated with electrical stimulation reaching three specific white matter pathways: the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists at Mount Sinai have identified three crucial brain connections associated with long-term improvement in patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) for severe depression that has not responded to conventional treatments. The discovery could help researchers make this experimental therapy more precise and effective.

Published October 1 in the American Journal of Psychiatry, the research examined the largest group of patients assembled across multiple independent cohorts to date who had received subcallosal cingulate deep brain stimulation (SCC DBS) for treatment-resistant depression.

The researchers found that lasting improvements were consistently associated with electrical stimulation reaching three specific white matter pathways: the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.

These findings strengthen the case for using detailed maps of the brain's connections to determine exactly where electrodes should be implanted, rather than choosing their positions based primarily on anatomical landmarks. Known as connectome-based targeting, this strategy has already helped shape the ongoing Abbott TRANSCEND clinical trial, a randomized, controlled study that uses individualized brain connectivity maps to guide SCC DBS treatment.

According to recent reports, "This study underscores the importance of individualized surgical targeting for achieving optimal outcomes with deep brain stimulation for depression," remarked Helen Mayberg, MD, Mount Sinai Professor in Neurotherapeutics and founding Director of the Nash Family Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. "In any randomized controlled trial of a neuromodulation treatment, precise lead placement and confirmation that the intended brain target has been engaged are essential first steps. We still have much to learn about which patients are most likely to benefit from stimulation of this particular target, but developing imaging-based signatures that can match patients to their optimal treatment remains a central goal of our research.".

How Deep Brain Stimulation Targets Severe Depression.

In a recent development, for people with treatment-resistant depression, standard therapies have failed to provide adequate relief. Researchers are investigating deep brain stimulation as a possible treatment for individuals living with severe, persistent symptoms.

The procedure involves surgically placing electrodes inside the brain to deliver controlled electrical signals to circuits involved in depression. However, positioning the electrodes correctly remains one of the greatest challenges.

Recent findings suggest that electrical stimulation does not simply affect the brain tissue closest to an implanted electrode. It can also influence larger networks through the white matter pathways that connect different brain regions. As a result, two patients with electrodes implanted in nearly identical locations may experience very different outcomes depending on which connections are actually stimulated.

Earlier research from Mount Sinai and Emory University helped establish the importance of these networks. In studies published between 2014 and 2023 in Biological Psychiatry, Molecular Psychiatry, and Nature, the teams identified white matter pathways associated with successful SCC DBS treatment and developed a method for planning electrode placement using brain connectivity maps.

Sources indicate that the latest investigation sought to determine whether those connections were also notable in patients treated at other research centers. Scientists also wanted to understand whether differences in the pathways reached by stimulation could help account for patients who did not benefit.

Three Brain Connections Linked to Lasting Improvement.

To investigate, the researchers examined information from several clinical studies, including the BROADEN trial and a patient cohort at the University of Toronto, where SCC DBS was originally developed.

They used computer models of the electrical fields generated by implanted electrodes alongside maps of brain connectivity. This allowed them to estimate which pathways received stimulation and compare those patterns across different patient groups.

The results showed a consistent relationship between sustained improvement and stimulation of the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.

It has been revealed that one finding was especially notable. Across the study sites, patients who had not responded to treatment after two years demonstrated a lack of stimulation engagement with the left cingulum bundle.

The researchers did not investigate whether moving electrodes to reach this pathway would improve those patients' symptoms. Nevertheless, the pattern offers a possible explanation for why apparently similar electrode placements can produce different results. An electrode might be positioned in the correct general region but still fail to activate all the connections associated with lasting improvement.

"This study addresses an crucial question in DBS: not simply which area of the brain to stimulate, but which connections within that area need to be engaged," remarked Brian Kopell, MD, Director of the Center for Neuromodulation at Mount Sinai. "For a network disorder such as depression, millimeters can determine whether stimulation reaches the pathways we intend to modulate. Identifying and reproducibly engaging those pathways gives us a more precise surgical target and a framework for understanding why otherwise similar electrode placements may produce different clinical outcomes.".

Toward More Personalized Depression Treatments.

Although reaching these three pathways appears notable, the researchers emphasize that electrode placement alone is unlikely to determine whether a patient improves.

The investigation concentrated on identifying the brain connections that should receive stimulation. Additional studies are needed to determine which individuals are most likely to benefit from SCC DBS and how electrical stimulation should be adjusted as treatment continues.

Industry observers note that there were also limitations to the brain imaging data. Individual diffusion MRI scans, which can provide information about a person's white matter connections, were not available for every participant. Consequently, much of the analysis used generalized maps of brain connectivity rather than maps created specifically for each patient.

It has been revealed that for the Emory patient group, the researchers were able to compare results obtained from generalized connectivity maps with those based on individual diffusion imaging. Both approaches produced consistent findings, providing further support for the importance of the identified pathways. However, more research is needed to establish the value of patient-specific imaging.

Future investigations will explore whether additional brain imaging measurements, including white matter integrity and functional connectivity, can help identify suitable patients, improve electrode placement, and guide treatment settings.

Sources indicate that "Our findings show precisely engaging these white matter pathways is a critical first step toward sustained response," stated Ki Sueng Choi, PhD, Associate Professor, Imaging Core Leader at the Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at Mount Sinai, and corresponding author of the study. "The next step is to characterize abnormal functional and structural brain states along these pathways to build more detailed models for setting patient-specific stimulation parameters, including amplitude, frequency, and pulse width, for precision medicine.".

By combining increasingly detailed brain maps with personalized stimulation settings, scientists hope to better understand why some people experience lasting relief while others do not. The findings represent another step toward developing more targeted treatments for severe depression, although further clinical research is necessary to establish how much these approaches can improve outcomes.

Research Funding and Disclosures.

The research received support from the National Institutes of Health BRAIN Initiative through grant UH3NS103550, the Hope for Depression Research Foundation, and the DANA Foundation.

Abbott's Neuromodulation business supplied data from the BROADEN clinical trial but did not participate in designing or analyzing the current study.

Sources indicate that conflict of Interest Disclosures: Dr. Brian Kopell serves as a paid consultant to Abbott Laboratories.

Dr. Helen Mayberg is a named co-inventor of a method that uses deep brain stimulation (DBS) in a particular brain region (the subcallosal cingulate area) to treat treatment-resistant depression. The method was licensed to Abbott Laboratories. Dr. Mayberg has received royalty payments from Functional Neuroscience related to this technology and is eligible to receive additional payments in the future. She also serves as a paid consultant to Abbott Laboratories in connection with its clinical trials involving DBS for depression.

Dr. Ki Sueng Choi and Dr. Martijn Figee are also paid consultants to Abbott Laboratories.

According to recent reports, dr. Mayberg, Dr. Kopell, and Dr. Choi are named co-inventors on a patent application covering a technique for identifying optimal electrode placement in deep brain stimulation for depression. The patent application was filed through Mount Sinai, and the technology remains unlicensed. However, the approach has been used in the TRANSCEND clinical trial.

According to recent reports, materials provided by The Mount Sinai Hospital / Mount Sinai School of Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#68993. How to Stay Informed But Not Overwhelmed by Election News

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1723 w)
