📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you may recognize that quiet, inner pull that comes when you least expect it, perhaps as a sense of unease that makes you change looks at the last minute, only to find out later that you narrowly missed something dangerous. Or you may feel drawn toward certain people or places without quite knowing why, only to discover later that those connections opened doors to fresh opportunities.

Sometimes these signals feel obvious, like a burst of excitement in your chest or butterflies in your stomach. Other times, they show up as a quiet sense of simply knowing what to do. Whether they’re instantaneous or linger over time, they may be signs of your intuition in action.

If you don’t feel very in tune with your intuition, there’s good news: Each day, you have the opportunity to turn inward, notice your thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations, and listen to what your inner voice might be telling you. Over time, this practice of self-awareness can become a habit that helps you live more authentically and fully.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world.

It has been revealed that intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world. Our body’s sensory networks are always at work gathering information from our environment, finding patterns from past experiences, and directing our present-day thinking and decisions.

It has been revealed that through our senses, our nervous system gathers information and sends signals to the brain. Regions like the amygdala help us rapidly detect potential threats, while the prefrontal cortex, which handles complex reasoning and decision-making, helps us interpret information more deliberately.

Research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

According to recent reports, that first, quick assessment happens remarkably fast. For instance, research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

In a recent development, intuition differs from instinct, which involves automatic responses that can help protect us from danger, including reactions like fight, flight, or freeze. While instinctive responses are largely automatic, intuition draws on our past life experiences and learned patterns to help us make sense of what we encounter in daily life. Although both can feel immediate, intuitive judgments are not always accurate and may also reflect learned biases or assumptions.

Sources indicate that intuition can feel like a gut feeling that is hard to put into words. This is because our brain is able to look for patterns between old memories and present-day situations, using useful takeaways from the past to guide us now. This process can also include implicit, unconscious memories that we may have thought we’d forgotten.

If the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?”.

If the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?” Part of the explanation lies in the gut-brain axis, the complex communication network connecting our brain and digestive system. The walls of our digestive tract contain a network of millions of neurons that make up the enteric nervous system, or ENS.

In a recent development, the ENS is often called our “second brain” because it can regulate many digestive functions independently of the central nervous system. Through the gut-brain axis, digestive processes can also interact with systems involved in mood and emotion. Research has linked gastrointestinal inflammation and changes in gut function with symptoms of depression and anxiety. Most of the body’s serotonin is also produced in the digestive tract, although it doesn’t directly enter the brain. Researchers are still exploring the complex relationship between gut health and mental well-being.

This gut-brain connection helps explain why we might experience a sinking feeling in the pit of our stomach when something doesn’t feel quite right.

All day long, our minds are hard at work integrating rational thought with emotional intelligence (EQ). EQ helps us to become aware of and understand both our emotions and those of others. It’s a type of intelligence we can develop through emotion regulation practice, expanding our emotional vocabulary, and approaching feelings as clues to something instead of an end product.

To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively.

EQ can help us manage stress, notice our assumptions, and respond more thoughtfully to difficult emotions, such as those that arise after a tense conversation. It helps us pause and remain mindful during challenging moments, and also as we choose our next steps. Developing emotional intelligence may also support our ability to recover from stressful experiences.

In Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), combining emotional awareness with rational thinking is known as accessing our wise mind. To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively. Instead of automatically acting on our first reaction, we can ground ourselves while tackling emotionally painful situations.

Wisdom and living authentically are closely connected.

Industry observers note that wisdom and living authentically are closely connected. As the ancient Greek maxim “Know thyself” suggests, self-knowledge is an important part of wisdom. By understanding our deeper motivations, core needs, and cherished values, we can make more intentional decisions that reflect who we are and what matters most to us.

Family systems therapist Virginia Satir connected personal authenticity to congruence between our internal reality and outward actions. This alignment can support our emotional well-being and help us act in ways that reflect our values. Incongruence, however, may leave us with a nagging sense that things are not quite right. Noticing incongruence in real time can help us to adjust and choose to do what feels more authentic to us and who we wish to be.

In a recent development, sometimes, traumatic experiences can make it harder to recognize or trust our intuition, particularly when painful memories leave us feeling fearful or unsafe. Common trauma responses, such as hypervigilance to danger, will tax our nervous system, making it difficult to access the balanced perspective of our wise mind.

Trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks.

Trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks. Similarly, depression can affect our self-esteem and confidence, informing how we interpret new situations as more negative. Holding hope for a better future might require noticing the positive patterns that run through our lives, and accessing support to process what we have gone through.

Social pressure can also make us second-guess ourselves. For example, growing up with family expectations to defer to others and put their needs first might make us believe that prioritizing our own needs is selfish. Similarly, other people’s ideas of what success looks like can make us overlook our own aspirations, such as the desire to pursue a different career path.

Industry observers note that we may become more aware of these pressures as we get older. Hospice nurse Bronnie Ware identified five common regrets her patients shared toward the end of their lives:.

These reflections offer a reminder of the importance of making choices that align with what matters most to us.

Getting to know ourselves—our preferences, desires, and even dreams—requires making time to turn inward. A helpful practice for building the habit of self-reflecting is time in peaceful solitude. Time alone may encourage mind-wandering and daydreaming, activities associated with the brain’s default mode network, which plays a role in reflection, imagination, and our sense of self.

Recent findings suggest that quiet may even have benefits for brain health. In one study, mice exposed to periods of silence developed more immature neurons in the hippocampus, a region involved in memory and learning. Though similar effects haven’t been established in humans, the presence of young neurons in the mice is a sign of brain plasticity. And while quiet moments may sometimes feel boring, they can also create space for reflection, creativity and new ideas.

Other practices, such as spending time in nature, journaling, meditation, engaging in spiritual reflection, and limiting technology, may also strengthen our intuition and self-awareness, as we remember who we are and what we care about the most.

Clarity about our personal values is another entryway to deepening intuition. In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), values help guide meaningful action and provide direction as we navigate life’s uncertainties. They can guide our daily actions much like an inner compass would—keeping us focused on long-term goals.

Sources indicate that knowing our values helps us remember how we want to show up during challenging times and stay grounded when stress feels overwhelming. Values can take many forms, from nurturing relationships, to cultivating personal qualities, or finding greater joy and fulfillment in everyday life. Naming your values and writing them down may help you distinguish between choices rooted in what matters to you and those driven primarily by fear, particularly when clarity feels hard to find.

In a recent development, psychotherapy can provide an intentional, supportive space where you can go inward. Therapy can also help us explore how past experiences shape our reactions, making it easier to distinguish familiar emotional patterns from what we’re noticing in the present. There are many evidence-based therapies that can help support trauma recovery, managing symptoms of anxiety and depression, and building a stronger sense of self:.

Each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves.

Thinking back to the gut feelings we began with—the caution that turned out to be right, and the inner pull that led toward new possibilities—we can see how these experiences may reflect more than coincidence. Instead, they’re signs that our nervous system, emotional intellect, mental pattern-finding, and lived experience are all working together to shape our perceptions and decisions.

Sources indicate that learning to trust our intuition’s guidance can take practice, particularly if difficult experiences have caused us to doubt it. But each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves. Over time, what once felt like a faint signal may become a steady, recognizable voice that helps us move forward with greater confidence. Our capacity for intuitive wisdom is always there, and the invitation is simply to listen.

Sources indicate that marian Ting, LMFT, is a therapist and writer specializing in mood disorders, complex trauma, and AAPI mental health. She is pursuing a PhD in depth psychology at Pacifica Graduate Institute, with research interests in the synergies between self-compassion and authentic selfhood. Her writing has been published by Psychotherapy Networker, the Anxiety and Depression Association of America, and Psychedelic Support, among others. She believes beauty and struggle can coexist, and that honest self-reflection is a form of healing.

Nomad art and design fair lands at Abu Dhabi’s Modernist former airport terminal

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom.
  • “Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” indicates the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte.
  • Simone Crestani’s Forsythia (2026), on show with Lebanese art and design gallery PIK’D at Nomad Abu Dhabi Courtesy PIK’D and NOMAD Abu Dhabi 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom. One such building is the decommissioned Terminal 1 of Zayed International Airport, which was designed by the French architect Paul Andreu and opened in 1982. Now a designated heritage site, it is the unique venue for the Abu Dhabi edition of the itinerant art and design fair Nomad (18-22 November), which returns to the city for a second time in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism.

“Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” indicates the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte. “[Terminal 1] has a very particular architecture, but also a history as a place of movement and exchange. Rather than placing conventional booths inside it, we wanted to work with the building as we found it—its terminals, corridors, scale and different spatial conditions—and allow those qualities to become part of how the works are experienced.”.

Simone Crestani’s Forsythia (2026), on show with Lebanese art and design gallery PIK’D at Nomad Abu Dhabi Courtesy PIK’D and NOMAD Abu Dhabi 2026.

This year, the fair is expanding that mission with ambitious site-specific takeovers of four of the airport’s private terminals by Nilufar gallery, Gallery Fumi, Galerie Gastou and the jewellery advisory firm A2Z. There are 50 exhibitors taking part this year (compared with 40 last year) including local returning participants such as Leila Heller Gallery and the A/P Room as well as international spaces like Paris-based Galerie BSL, Milan’s Galleria Rossana Orlandi and Carpenters Workshop Gallery from London.

Highlights at the fair will include Maison Intègre’s bronze objects made using the ancient technique of lost wax, cast from recycled metal at its foundry in Burkina Faso; Seoul-based gallery Vein’s pairing of contemporary Korean practices with traditions including ottchil lacquer and mother-of-pearl inlay; and Polish design from Craftica Gallery.

Sources indicate that bellavance‑Lecompte states that jewellery will also be in the spotlight—as well as the 450 sq. m exhibition by A2Z, there will be presentations from the designers Studio Renn, Mattar jewellers and the gallery and advisory Ars Belga/Matthu-Boghossian. The Belgian jewellers Levuma will collaborate with the London gallery JCRD Design to bring together fine jewellery, diamonds and Brazilian design.

Another vital development for Nomad this year is its expanded roster of institutions and non-profit initiatives on show in the old airport’s departure hall. Joining Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council—a Sharjah-based organisation that works with female artisans from the UAE and the wider Middle East, North Africa, South and Southeast Asia regions—which returns for this edition, is the recently established Design Commission Abu Dhabi and a collaborative presentation from the Institut du Monde Arabe (IMA) in Paris and House of Artisans, a cultural centre in Abu Dhabi that preserves traditional Emirati crafts. The project will bring together the French Sudanese fashion designer Abdel El Tayeb, who won the Confirmed Talent category of IMA’s 2024 Design Prize, and Emirati artisans to create a site-specific installation. “[This project] speaks to an idea at the heart of this edition: craft is a living practice, and something upcoming can emerge when makers from different places work together,” Bellavance‑Lecompte indicates.

For Nomad’s inaugural Abu Dhabi edition, galleries reported sales exceeding $20m and many are “returning this year with more ambitious projects”, Bellavance‑Lecompte claims. He expects that Abu Dhabi’s expanding cultural calendar and soon-to-open Guggenheim museum will bring more international collectors, curators and attention to the city and to Nomad. “Last year showed us that there is serious interest in collectable design, and this year we can build on those relationships,” he says.

• Nomad Abu Dhabi, Old Abu Dhabi Airport, 18-22 November.

Breaking: Vinny Ferraro: Healing Our Pain with Loving-Kindness

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that very often, the thought of practicing a kind, friendly presence that allows us to connect with pain rather than turn away from it seems counter-intuitive, doesn’t it?
  • We are the ancestors of the nervous animals, so achieving a kind of intimacy with our difficulties doesn’t exactly come naturally.
  • According to recent reports, add to that, the many ways to opt out of actually caring for ourselves in our contemporary culture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that very often, the thought of practicing a kind, friendly presence that allows us to connect with pain rather than turn away from it seems counter-intuitive, doesn’t it? Generally, when we come into contact with something painful or scary, our habitual tendency is to push it away, and to try to get away from it out of self-preservation. This is not your fault. This is biology.

We are the ancestors of the nervous animals, so achieving a kind of intimacy with our difficulties doesn’t exactly come naturally. It’s hard for us to imagine that the things we’ve been battling with our whole lives could be sources of awakening. And it’s so easy to judge our experiences, essentially holding it against ourselves that we are the way we are.

According to recent reports, add to that, the many ways to opt out of actually caring for ourselves in our contemporary culture. Maybe we worry we’re being self-indulgent or even come to see ourselves as inconveniences. It’s so easy to slip into judgment.

In a recent development, with compassion practice we open up to this tender space. And when that opening happens, we find there’s actually room for the life that’s right here, right now. So, I ask you to go easy on yourself as we venture into this territory of giving ourselves compassion.

What is the real cost of being at war with ourselves, or some part of ourselves?

Sources indicate that we come by it all so honestly. But let’s explore: What is the real cost of being at war with ourselves, or some part of ourselves? And what does it really feel like when we wage that war? How much are our experiences bringing to us, and how much are we bringing to our experiences?

Consider this: Our response to whatever arises is where we put our attention—that’s what we actually have influence over. We can’t control what arises. We do have some power over where we place our attention.

Sources indicate that many practitioners talk about this in terms of the “second arrow.” That’s when we take something that’s already difficult and multiply that by our resistance to it. And this can be far more painful than the initial feeling itself.

This is the formula: Experience x Resistance = Suffering.

Recent findings suggest that so, how do we hold ourselves with some compassion? “Suffering” is a really major word. In light of all that’s going on in the world, it’s easy to feel like we can dismiss what we’re dealing with personally. But I think we have to include ourselves and whatever difficulties we’re dealing with. The mind is always saying, “Well, at least, you know, at least…”—and you fill in the blank. At least it’s not this, at least it’s not that. I don’t know about you, but I can feel kind of bullied into gratitude when I’m not willing to meet what’s difficult with some compassion. Let’s accept, then, that resistance is normal. Resistance gets to be here, too.

Sources indicate that pain can be in our lives in countless ways—and all of it is difficult. Each one of us has been touched by grief, loss, countless struggles. Those things in and of themselves are difficult for many of us to navigate. But even harder than those things is when we regard what has happened, or is happening, as our fault.

We don’t have to defend our pain or judge ourselves. I see it with my two-year-old son. Sometimes he’s just screaming. Something is just really, really bothering him. It doesn’t matter what it is. I know what he needs. He needs a hug. He needs to be held. He needs care. He needs loving attention.

In a recent development, that’s what we’re going to do in this practice: hold ourselves with that same kind of care. We’re going to allow ourselves to kiss our own wounds the way we would for anyone we care about.

Industry observers note that we start with a willingness to have contact with the pain and soften to it, not resist it. We do that by tuning into our body and the sensations that are present. Is there a temperature shift? A throbbing? Is it moving? Is there a centre; are their edges? Are there places that it’s not?

Industry observers note that if it becomes overwhelming, we can allow our awareness to go to the part of our experience that’s not activated. We can visit where this pain lives in our bodies, and we can come back to a place of calm if it gets to be too much.

Bringing our curiosity to this is key. Not “why is this happening to me?” or the story we might be building around it, but what is the felt sense of this pain? This is the power of mindfulness—the ability to cultivate a clearer view of what’s coming up and therefore not be blindsided by it or lost in it.

Sources indicate that we’re looking for two components in this practice, then: willingness and seeing clearly. Simply put, when we bring compassion home to include ourselves, our job is to honor the hurt. This isn’t easy. In fact, it’s very rare for us to meet ourselves in that place. But if we don’t, we’re losing out on living a considerable portion of our lives.

Industry observers note that as we talked about last week, the initiative here is to widen our circle of care as we go. We started with those dearest to us; now we’re going focus on ourselves. Next week we will hold neutral people in mind and then we’ll hold everyone, including difficult people. I love the sequence, but sometimes I feel like when I’m practicing, I can be all four of those categories of people. Sometimes I’m an easy person to care about. Sometimes it’s difficult to hold myself with compassion. Sometimes I feel pretty neutral.

I encourage you to reflect on when you feel you need love the most. For me, it’s particularly when I mess up. And when we don’t feel like we can meet ourselves, isn’t that when we really see what kind of lovers we are? Is it conditional—is it as long as I act right? What we want to do here is widen the berth of where we’re willing to meet ourselves.

Recent findings suggest that I want to re-emphasize here: It’s important not to use any part of the practice to judge ourselves. What we’re trying to do is give ourselves a pardon. This is how we can meet ourselves where we feel most unmet.

I find it helpful to note what’s arising as I’m doing this compassion practice. It helps me to see better what my relationship is to that pain. This also helps me to see this as something that’s passing through my awareness. It’s not who I am. I find that distinction very helpful.

Recent findings suggest that to put it another way, we’re trying not to take any of this personally. We realize we can practice with just about anything if we’re not taking it personally. Whether it’s stress, frustration, pain: nothing has to be outside our care. Maybe we feel like we’ve been through too much pain, or not enough—it doesn’t really matter why we’re in pain, just that we can acknowledge that there is stuff that is painful.

Industry observers note that remember, too, that we’re inviting spaciousness around this pain we’re finding. The pain is not the only thing happening here. This is the alchemy of presence. It helps us approach the very difficulties that we’ve been desperately trying to avoid so that they can become the sources of our awakening, of our wisdom, of equanimity.

OK, let’s stop reading the menu and eat some of the food.

Read and practice the guided meditation script below, pausing after each paragraph. Or listen to the audio practice.

Be on the lookout for where compassion arises in your life, in the day to day. Locate where compassion arises naturally and where it could use some cultivation. Try spending some time each day reflecting on your heart’s intention in this practice.

Industry observers note that vinny Ferraro has been a practitioner of insight meditation (vipassanā) since the early 1990s. He is a co-Founder of the Dharma Punx and co-Guiding Teacher of Against the Stream Buddhist Meditation Society. He is also a nationally recognized leader in designing and implementing interventions for at-risk adolescents and is currently Senior Trainer for Mindful Schools. In 1987, he began leading groups in drug rehabilitation centers, juvenile halls, and halfway houses. In 2001, he began teaching for Challenge Day, a nationally recognized, social & emotional learning program, eventually becoming their Director of Training and leading workshops for over 110,000 youth on four continents. Vinny is also a board member and former Training Director of the Mind Body Awareness Project and is the principal author of MBA’s mindfulness-based curriculum for incarcerated youth. Vinny has received national media coverage for his work with adults and youth; his work is the subject of the MTV series “If You Really Knew Me…”.

Located in the heart of the Mexican city of Hermosillo, Sonora, you will find Champ, a small boutique hotel. The street on which it is located is Campodónico, the surname of recognized waltz composer Rodolfo Campodónico, born in Hermosillo in 1866. He garnered a lot of recognition for his work during the early 20th century and his nickname was “Champ,” and that is from where the hotel took its name.

Champ celebrates the desert, the city, the local spirit and Sonoran traditions. Using imagery from old postcards and photos found in basements and thrift shops, its aim is to be as cozy and comfortable as possible for its guests.

In a recent development, the muted color palette was inspired by the arid northern Mexican region, where the vastness of the land and the sky reign supreme. A retro typography was chosen, since the old house where Champ is located was built in the 1970s.

Typefaces used: Pitch by Klim Type Foundry Galey by Prestigetype Studio Saa Series by URW Type Foundry Helvetica by Max Miedinger and Eduard Hoffmann Century 725 by Heinrich Wilhelm Hoffmeister.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Turner Duckworth kept the hand-dipped red top exactly where it belongs, at the center of the system, then built a whole language out of it.
  • In a recent development, the type comes from a person, not a library.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turner Duckworth rebuilt the Maker's Mark brand identity around its red wax, casting Star Hill Farm materials into marks that tell the story.

The bottle does the talking. Turner Duckworth kept the hand-dipped red top exactly where it belongs, at the center of the system, then built a whole language out of it. Wheat stalks, oak rings and native flora from Star Hill Farm were dipped and cast in the same red wax, so the marks that carry the brand are literal pieces of the place. Against a Wheat Cream ground, the red reads as one loud note in a quiet room, with Printmaker's Black holding the type steady.

In a recent development, the type comes from a person, not a library. Co-founder Margie Samuels shaped the original bottle, and the studio recreated her handwriting as a custom typeface with Nick Cooke at G-Type. Hundreds of characters, contextual alternates and ligatures keep it feeling handwritten rather than set, and her voice runs through the labels, menus and posters in a flowing, wax-like hand.

Layouts stay plain on purpose. A letterhead puts the Samuels family's SIV mark at the center and the distillery address in the corner, so place sits at the heart of every sheet. Type stays large and calm, with room around it, and the wordmark does its work without decoration.

In a recent development, the palette is the bottle, remembered in three tones. Wheat Cream is the ground, true to the label. Printmaker's Black carries the type. Wax Red does the rest, in finish and in form: powder-coated metal, glazing and varnish applied to objects with smooth, flowing shapes. The same red runs across mugs, folders, books and table tents, so every object in the world feels dipped from the same pot.

In a recent development, scott Grummett photographed the world at Star Hill Farm in warm cream tones and natural light, with touches of glossy wax red. The pictures tell the slower story behind the liquid: hand-rotated barrels, hand-cut labels, hand-dipped bottles, and the land that gives it flavour.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Auto racing’s seen an explosion of flimsy “fashion wheel” brands that pretend to be high-performance.
  • In a recent development, we started by naming the problem that Apex solves, calling it The Great Knowledge Void.
  • To stop people from buying bogus wheels.

Auto racing’s seen an explosion of flimsy “fashion wheel” brands that pretend to be high-performance. Apex is different — engineering elite racing wheels at an unmatched price point. But when we met them, customers were completely unaware of the difference. Working closely with their CEO, Eddy Pintacsi, we developed a newly introduced category vision and brand, positioning them as the category leader they are, and injecting some much-needed truth into the wheel industry.

In a recent development, we started by naming the problem that Apex solves, calling it The Great Knowledge Void. A state of play where any wheel brand can make performance claims — true or not — just to make a buck. And the worst part? Customers have no way to know the difference. We went on to tell a story of how Apex is fixing this problem with their core ethos: “Real performance.” A pledge to show customers the truth — or die trying. End of story.

The identity is loud and urgent. To stop people from buying bogus wheels. The arching curves and high-contrast colors catch the eyes on the track — where it matters. And we worked with Apex to weave the same sense of urgency into how they talk about their testing standards. So that the entire industry would get with the program.

Altogether, the rebrand, POV, and messaging proves that Apex stands alone in its category. We call this a “Category of One” brand. Because when you risk everything on the track, there’s only one thing you can trust — Real Performance.

It’s Selfish, It’s Hokey, and I’ll Lose My Edge: 3 Half-Truths About Self-Compassion

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’m a late adopter of a lot of things.
  • It has been revealed that why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion?
  • It has been revealed that we think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’m a late adopter of a lot of things. It took me two years to get an iPhone, a lot of convincing to wear AirPods (which I still call ear pods despite my son’s cringe), and it took me even longer to drink the “self-compassion” Kool-Aid. (Which I guess I drank because I wrote a book on how to practice self-compassion daily!).

It has been revealed that why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion? I believed three things about self-compassion that turned me off. But I’ve since learned, they are really only half-truths.

It has been revealed that we think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused. Yet the research highlights that when you practice self-compassion, you are more likely to:.

If you are a parent, you probably know this firsthand. When you practice caring for yourself, you are less likely to have your stress spill over onto your kids. But there is a half-truth to self-compassion making you selfish.

According to recent reports, in other words, if you are worried that self-compassion will make you selfish, focus more on how giving yourself compassion will help you be of service to others. One body-based practice I like to do with this concept is a simple breathing exercise:.

Breathing in, I take in care and understanding.Breathing out, I send out care and understanding.

There is a large body of research showing that self-compassion actually helps you perform better, not worse.

Self-compassion helps you stay on track with your wisest values and goals. The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion you may choose to lose your edge a little…in good ways.

It has been revealed that as you learn to listen more to your body and stop berating yourself for mistakes, you naturally may want to give up on pushing yourself in ways that are harmful. I’ve lost my edge when it comes to having to run every day, getting every email returned in a timely manner, and making the perfect dinner for my family (hello Trader Joe’s frozen aisle!) … and that’s a good thing.

Recent findings suggest that when my clients are struggling with whether or not they should push themselves at something, I ask them to do what contemplative leader Stephen Batchelor suggested to me: Drop the question into your belly. If you struggle with self-criticism or rigid rules, your belly is likely to have a more compassionate answer than your head!

It can feel uncomfortable to say nice things to yourself, and sometimes downright cheesy. I rarely recommend clients cheer themselves on with the “Good job” or “Way to go!” statements that some motivational coaches suggest.

Self-compassion is relating to yourself in a way that is encouraging, warm, realistic, and just right for you. You don’t need to recite a list of loving-kindness mantras or put your hand on your heart if you find those practices hokey. Sometimes self-compassion is as simple as noticing the part of you that is scared and being with it a little longer.

The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion, you just might start to adopt some hokey platitudes toward yourself. But hey, they are platitudes for a good reason, right?

In a recent development, to learn more about how to bring self-compassion into your daily life, read The Self-Compassion Daily Journal by Dr. Diana Hill or listen to the Wise Effort Podcast.

Diana Hill, PhD is a clinical psychologist, international trainer and sought-out speaker on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and compassion. Host of the Wise Effort podcast, author of The Self-Compassion Daily Journal, and co-author the ACT Daily Journal. @drdianahill.

  • Since it all began with two determined women in a Sydney-side backyard shed in 2007, The Dinner Ladies have been filling the freezers, bellies and hearts of thousands of busy Australian families with their ready-to-heat comfort meals.
  • The market for pre-prepared meal delivery is an oversaturated landscape steeped in clichés and same-same messaging that claims to be the most healthy, convenient or delicious dinnertime solution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Dinner Ladies needed a recipe for a rebrand that would not only pay respect to their unique origin story but bring their visual and verbal identity up to speed with their growth as Australia’s tastiest frozen meal service. We joined forces to cook them up a fresh look and feel that reflects their homely meals and anti-“mumsy” attitude, extending all the way from their website through to their packaging. Now whack the oven on, because Australia’s hottest frozen meal service has arrived.

Since it all began with two determined women in a Sydney-side backyard shed in 2007, The Dinner Ladies have been filling the freezers, bellies and hearts of thousands of busy Australian families with their ready-to-heat comfort meals. Born from a deep understanding of dinner time chaos, and the desire to bring some ease back into this routine, The Dinner Ladies’ commitment to delivering meals worthy of mum’s tick of approval remains unwavering.

The market for pre-prepared meal delivery is an oversaturated landscape steeped in clichés and same-same messaging that claims to be the most healthy, convenient or delicious dinnertime solution. They not only lack a distinct personality but also relatability to their customer — time-poor people who just want simple, genuinely good, homemade meals that help take the pressure off when it’s needed most. This is where The Dinner Ladies shine. A flavour-stacked service that takes care of dinner, so you can focus on doing life.

In a recent development, the brand had become known and loved for their unexpected, no nonsense and slightly audacious approach. This was not only refreshingly real but a reflection of both their wholesome offering and the founding ladies. However, over seventeen years of brand iterations their look had become diluted, lost its attitudinal punch, and needed a big serve of reinvigoration. Our vision was to bring back the best from their history and turn up the heat across the board to let the nation know they mean (meal delivery) business.

We fully immersed ourselves in The Dinner Ladies story, from taking a deep dive through past website designs and hand drawn logos on a napkin, to visiting the shed where it all began and the factory where it now thrives. This helped us draw out the strongest existing brand elements, like their early trad-tattoo-esque illustrations and counter-“mumsy” stereotype, and turn them into a modern evolution. Driven by “Food from the Heart,” each component of the visual identity communicates the brand essence and no-BS confidence of a service that truly helps take the stress out of dinnertime.

The first step was the refinement of the logo. By decoupling the heart and the script, we gave it flexibility, made it easier to read at every touchpoint and allowed it to scale as needed. The custom heart logo was designed by us and then, alongside the wordmark, handed to illustrator Jake Foreman to redraw and personalise with his iconic texture and gritty stipple.

The Dinner Ladies’ existing red already had distinct brand attribution in the category so we just refined it with a bright and modern twist. The secondary palette supports our hero red with a balance of warm, approachable and slightly retro hues. When united, the system unlocks a number of interesting and vibrant combinations that are particularly useful across hard-working digital applications.

We used the typeface Denim by Displaay Type Foundry to show off the brand’s confident personality yet retain practicality. Denim Wide’s used in headings and call-to-action applications to command attention, while its regular cut counterpart rounds out the system with a friendly, clean and legible option for subheadings and body copy. With its subtle details, the typeface can be an attention-grabbing hero element that showcases the bold tone of voice but also work alongside more expressive moments.

Recent findings suggest that the tone of voice needed to capture the brand’s joyful, cheeky yet comforting personality, while steering clear of any patronising “mumsy” tropes and stereotypes. We worked with copywriter Cat Wall to develop a verbal identity that balanced the empathetic caregiver with the charmingly rebellious tone of the ladies themselves. In a category saturated with over-sincerity and fake friendliness, the tone offers a refreshing sprinkle of irreverence with a straight-forward, bull-free reflection of the audience and their needs.

Sources indicate that the photography celebrates the authentic messiness of real life dinnertime. A reflection of the brand’s tell-it-like-it-is attitude, the shoot didn’t shy away from capturing raw moments — the remnants of a great dish alongside a newly introduced one being served or a bolognese-faced baby — mixed with the joy of sharing generous, mouth-watering food.

Sources indicate that with Alana Dimou behind the lens, Jerrie-Joy Redman-Lloyd on styling, Oriana De Luca on wardrobe, Gavin Anesbury with a hair and makeup brush in hand, and Michaela Le on production, the brand came to life. Warm, natural lighting, combined with quirky styling choices, pops of colour or pattern and intentional (and encouraged) chaos set a homely and inviting scene with a pinch of rebellion.

Illustration has always been a major piece of The Dinner Ladies’ brand so we wanted to bring it across to the rebrand. The original illustrations’ punk and rough-around-the-edges flair drew us to references of traditional trad tattoos.

In a recent development, collaborating further with illustrator Jake Foreman, we crafted a suite of illustrations that served as both personality-rich storytelling pieces and functional devices. While the small scenes and spots speak to specific offerings of the brand, the hero illustration speaks to the love behind every Dinner Ladies dish and the comforting shared experiences created around the table.

These illustrations are supported by our suite of type-furniture elements that not only support the main design elements but add character to any layout.

As a product that’s often shoved into the freezer and then reached for in a rush, legibility and easy differentiation were priorities for designing the packaging. A simple colour-coded system helps to distinguish between protein groups at a glance, making it quick and effortless to find the crowd-pleasing meal that’s ready to save the day.

The Dinner Ladies now have a brand that not only celebrates their seventeen year legacy but gives them the tools for future decades of success. The flexible design system and punchy tone of voice pays tribute to their tenacious past, the founding ladies behind the service and their wholesome mission put joy back into dinner time. Now The Dinner Ladies can stand loud and proud with a brand that reflects their readiness to dish up delicious dinners to an entire nation.

Seven reveals to see in the UAE during Frieze Abu Dhabi

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.
  • Industry observers note that in What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory.
  • The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.

Industry observers note that in What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory. Through a series of sculptural works, etchings and drawings, Al Mubarak strives to recall specific places and objects from her own childhood, embracing the distortions of memory. A monumental sandcastle evokes a child’s perspective of space, while bubble wrap that has been compulsively popped or left intact is cast in resin, turning a disposable material into an enduring sculptural form.

The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.

Emirati artist Shaikha Al Mazrou at the Cultural Foundation, where she is staging a solo show Courtesy the Cultural Foundation.

Cultural Foundation, Abu Dhabi, 12 November-15 March 2027.

According to recent reports, in 2022, Shaikha Al Mazrou presented her large-scale work Red Stack as part of Frieze Sculpture in London’s Regent’s Park. The work exemplifies her deft approach to defying perceptions through her choice of materials. It features a pile of red cushions constructed from fibreglass and resin on a metal framework. Despite the hardness of the materials, the creased and pillowy cushions evoke a sense of softness.

She receives her strongest spotlight to date with her solo exhibition at the Abu Dhabi’s Cultural Foundation. It will feature past work alongside newly introduced commissions created specifically for the venue’s atrium. Al Mazrou’s work is also on view at Frieze Abu Dhabi with Lawrie Shabibi.

In a recent development, installation view: All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, 2026. Pictured here: Rand Abdul Jabbar, Earthly Wonders, Celestial Beings (series), (2024).

NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Abu Dhabi, until 3 January 2027.

In 1951, Jewad Selim and Shakir Hassan Al Stated established a movement that sought to express Modernist art principles through a uniquely Iraqi perspective. It would prove to be one of the most defining moments of Arab art.

All Manner of Experiments is perhaps the most comprehensive survey of the Baghdad Modern Art Group. It presents seminal works from the period as well as contemporary pieces that highlight the ongoing legacies of the group.

The exhibition at the New York University (NYU) Abu Dhabi Art Gallery brings together works from 1946 to 2023, from private and institutional collections. Selim’s experiments with abstraction are represented, as well as Al Stated’s figurative expressions and his latter work that employed Arabic letters to convey an inner dimension. Key works by Dia al-Azzawi, Madiha Umar and Khalid al-Rahal are also presented, with the exhibition concluding with contemporary pieces by Mahmoud Obaidi, Walid Siti and Rand Abdul Jabbar, among others.

A key point of departure in this show is Selim’s Freedom Monument, a 50m-long sculpture in Tahrir Square that was commissioned just after the 1958 military coup that overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and established the Iraqi Republic. Though Selim died in 1961 before the sculpture fully materialised, it is considered to be one of his most enduring works, potent with the sensibilities that inspired the Baghdad Modern Art Group. Read from right to left—like an Arabic text—the monument tells the story of the revolution. Its bronze figures draw from Sumerian motifs while also employing Modernist aesthetics.

A carved ivory jewelled casket on show in the exhibition Spices and Wonders at Louvre Abu Dhabi © Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi; Photo: Sylvie Van Roey.

Louvre Abu Dhabi, until 14 February 2027.

According to recent reports, the Indian Ocean has been a pivotal node of cultural exchange for centuries, and an exhibition at the Louvre Abu Dhabi unravels the ancient maritime connections that linked Europe, Africa and the Middle East to South and Southeast Asia. Held in collaboration with the Guimet Museum in Paris, the exhibition charts these links through artefacts, textiles, ceramics and spices.

Recent findings suggest that this investigation extends to Art Here—a staple show in Louvre Abu Dhabi’s calendar, presenting works shortlisted for the annual Richard Mille Art Prize. This year’s exhibition, exploring the theme of “Confluences” is curated by Kamini Sawhney (until 28 February 2027).

Sources indicate that serendipitously, the theme of Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi also looks towards the Indian Ocean, presenting artefacts, maps and rare books. Presentations at Frieze will contribute to research into an understudied historical topic with implications for the modern era.

Luisa Dörr, various works from Escaramuzas, (2024–ongoing).

Photography Gallery, Sharjah, until 29 November.

The 13th edition of Vantage Point takes place at the Photography Gallery in Sharjah, a venue that opened in November 2025. The exhibition, an annual fixture in Sharjah’s arts programme since 2013, is being held in an overhauled format. Each year, dozens of international artists have taken part in the exhibition, which celebrates photographic works across genres, from photojournalism to more experimental compositions. Vantage Point has now been pared down, exhibiting commissioned works by six photographers, and it will also be a biennial event moving forward.

In a recent development, sathish Kumar presents a series of images that focus on his brother, an oil worker in Abu Dhabi. Photographs of Kumar’s family in the industrial city compound in Al Ruwais are juxtaposed with those taken in Bengaluru in southern India. Much of the latter centre around the construction site of the family home. The series, titled Bond, alludes to the fraught experiences of many South Asian labourers who travel to the Gulf with the aim of financially supporting their parents and families back home.

The other works featured in the exhibition are equally evocative and personal. Latifa AlBokhari presents tender images that mark key moments in a woman’s life in the Gulf, from henna traditions to wedding preparations. Guanyu Xu highlights life-sized images of domestic interiors that offer clues to the personalities of the people that inhabit them. Luisa Dörr documents with painterly sensibilities a female-focused equestrian school in Mexico. Maheder Haileselassie spotlights archival images of Arbegnoch fighters, who resisted the Italian occupation of Ethiopia between 1936 and 1941. Finally, Adam Rouhana presents larger-than-life portraits of Palestinians from the West Bank, whom he photographed in a travelling studio.

Courtesy of the artist and ATHR Gallery.

The Jameel Arts Centre has given five artists each a dedicated space within the institution.

Industry observers note that one room charts four decades of Walid Siti's practice. Sketches of dark, spiralling towers embody the human pathology of scaling literal and proverbial heights. Sculptures and acrylic paintings of mountains, meanwhile, beckon to the peaks of his native Iraqi Kurdistan. A commissioned large-scale sculpture is the centrepiece of the exhibition. It outlines a mountain in stacked polystyrene, with writing on its underside that reflects on the turbulent history of Kurdistan.

Bahraini painter Lulua Alyahya presents the urban and natural environments of the Gulf with diffused brushstrokes. Her work often teeters on the absurd, with lions scowling from computer screens and chickens hatching eggs that fry on the pavement.

Afrah Shafiq is showing Nobody Knows For Certain, an interactive video game work that drawns on a lesser-known but rich period of cultural exchange between India and the Soviet Union that took place between the 1950s and 80s.

New Dream Machine Project, a three-metre-high installation by Shezad Dawood, is a gyrating tower pulsing with light. Inspired by Brion Gysin’s Dreamachine, which the artist devised after his time in Tangier and after “experimenting with altered states of being” with members of the Beat Generation. The installation was prototyped by artisans in Fes, Morocco, with the final version engineered in Slough, England.

Trembling Hands (2024) by Bani Abidi gathers the artist's portraits of artists, journalists and politicians who spoke out against the genocide of Palestinians, some of whom faced backlash, censorship or repression as a result.

Installation view of Rohini Devasher, Latent Fields (Field Five) (2023); Latent Fields (Field Six) (2023).

Ishara Art Foundation, Dubai, until 15 December.

The sky held it, the earth remembered presents the work of Pakistani artist Shahana Rajani, Indian artist Rohini Devasher and Bangladeshi artist Sarker Protick, all of whom consider how memory and history are preserved and transmitted.

In Rajani’s three-channel video Lines that World a River, a woman paints a house along the banks of a river. The scene is vibrant with its textured blues and chalky greens. Rajani zooms in on the woman’s fingers. Her nails are streaked with the white of the paint she uses to draw the river’s foam. The drawing is of the woman’s ancestral village along the Indus River Delta—now submerged after the construction of hydraulic dams and barrages.

The work—a new iteration of Rajani’s Four Acts of Recovery, which won the Han Nefkens Foundation’s inaugural South Asian Video Art Production Grant in 2023—shows how displaced communities in the Indus region have developed mural painting practices to remember their lost homes.

In a recent development, devasher’s Latent Fields comprises three sprawling silk panels that hang from the ceiling. Their dots and patterns allude to sunspots and other solar events, coming together as a monumental record of celestial time.

In Dhaka 1217, meanwhile, Protick presents 135 photographs that capture the transformation of the neighbourhood where the artist was born and continues to live.

Recent findings suggest that ashton was the first restaurant chain in Canada to specialize in poutine – it’s been serving the iconic dish since 1969. However, as the decades passed, both Ashton’s image and its restaurants remained frozen in time. In 2022, Émily Adam and Jean-Christophe Lirette took over the reins from Ashton Leblond, with a vision of expanding the 23 locations of this beloved Quebec brand.

The latest owners faced some major challenges: stagnant sales figures, outdated restaurants, an aging clientele and the need to recruit younger workers. It swiftly became clear that Ashton’s brand image and experience needed to be revitalized.

LG2 reimagined Ashton’s entire brand experience at one of its flagship restaurants. Numerous elements were redesigned to simplify the brand as a whole and turn it into an exportable entity.

It has been revealed that the experience was updated with a perfect blend of modernity and traditions rooted in Ashton’s history. In tribute to snack bar culture, all the classic codes of diners were integrated with a modern twist. A customized typographic signature emphasizing the generous, indulgent nature of Ashton dishes was created, and the chain’s signature red colour was updated. A touch of nostalgia can be felt in the latest brand merchandise, which features illustrations reminiscent of one of Ashton’s earliest logos.

The colours are rich, curved edges are prominent and the triple red line – inspired by the chain’s iconic neon lighting – runs through every touchpoint in the graphic system, from the fresh packaging to the stripes on socks.

To create an atmosphere as comforting as its food, the design concept was completely overhauled. This transformation can be seen from the outer shell to the interior details: the pervasive curves, neon lighting and red tin roof are all reminiscent of Ashton’s original 1969 food truck.

A monochrome red border runs through the dining room where the famous banquettes are still featured prominently in the centre. This easily reproducible layout will be extended to the chain’s other restaurants over the next few years.

It has been revealed that the numbers speak for themselves. Within 30 days of launch:.

35% increase in traffic at the first renovated location 34% increase in sales at the first renovated location 40% increase in visits to the Ashton website.

Ashton found the perfect recipe for securing the loyalty of diehard fans while attracting fresh foodies on the hunt for a retro yet contemporary experience.

Industry News: What Science Reveals About Gratitude’s Impact on the Brain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gratitude is celebrated throughout philosophy and religion; recent scientific studies suggest it carries significant benefits for our mental and physical health.
  • According to recent reports, why does that matter?
  • Better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gratitude is celebrated throughout philosophy and religion; recent scientific studies suggest it carries significant benefits for our mental and physical health. But very little is known about what actually happens in our brain and body when we experience it.

According to recent reports, why does that matter? Because better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits and help people understand the importance of fostering this powerful emotion. The goal of my research has been to lay the groundwork for understanding what happens in the brain when we feel grateful—and a picture of the grateful brain is now starting to emerge.

Better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits.

When I first embarked on the journey to study gratitude, I came across philosophical treatises and religious exhortations emphasizing the importance of gratitude, along with scientific studies suggesting that gratitude can improve your sleep, enhance your romantic relationships, protect you from illness, motivate you to exercise, and boost your happiness, among many other benefits.

Recent findings suggest that at the time, however, very little was known about what happens in our brains and bodies when we experience gratitude, which made it difficult to understand how gratitude actually works. Since I’m a neuroscientist, I zeroed in on the neurobiology of gratitude with a more specific question in mind: Can our brain activity reveal anything about how gratitude achieves its significant benefits?

Sources indicate that given the clear relationship between mental and physical health, I thought that understanding what happens in the brain when we feel gratitude could tell us more about the mind-body connection—namely, how feeling positive emotion can improve bodily functions. I also thought these results could help scientists design programs aimed at generating gratitude by helping them zero in on the precise activities and experiences most essential to reaping gratitude’s benefits.

Industry observers note that it must be said that actually capturing people in the moment of feeling gratitude poses some challenges. After all, some people may not feel gratitude when we expect them to, and others may even feel grateful in unexpected situations. I thought my best bet would be to try to induce gratitude through powerful stories of aid and sacrifice.

Industry observers note that to achieve this, I turned to the USC Shoah Foundation Institute for Visual History, which houses the world’s largest repository of videotaped Holocaust survivor testimonies—many of which, perhaps surprisingly, are filled with breathtaking acts of selflessness and generosity. Along with a team of amazing undergraduates, I began by watching hundreds of hours of survivor testimony to find stories in which the survivor received help of some kind from another person.

We assembled a collection of these stories and transformed them into short scenarios that we shared with our participants. Each scenario was re-phrased into the second-person (e.g., “You are on a wintertime death march and a fellow prisoner gives you a warm coat”) and presented to our study’s participants. We asked them to imagine themselves in the scenario and feel, as much as possible, how they would feel if they were in the same situation. While participants reflected on these gifts, we measured their brain activity using modern brain imaging techniques (in the form of functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI).

The regions associated with gratitude are part of the neural networks that light up when we socialize and experience pleasure.

For each of these scenarios, we asked participants how much gratitude they felt, and we correlated this rating with their brain activity in that moment. While such an approach will not elicit exactly the same feelings as actually living through such situations, participants overwhelmingly reported strong feelings of gratitude, deep engagement in the task, and, perhaps even more importantly, an increased empathy for and understanding of the Holocaust as a result of participating in the study.

In a recent development, what’s more, our results revealed that when participants reported those grateful feelings, their brains highlighted activity in a set of regions located in the medial pre-frontal cortex, an area in the frontal lobes of the brain where the two hemispheres meet. This area of the brain is associated with understanding other people’s perspectives, empathy, and feelings of relief. This is also an area of the brain that is massively connected to the systems in the body and brain that regulate emotion and support the process of stress relief.

These data told us a reasonable story about gratitude:.

According to recent reports, practicing gratitude has incredible effects, from improving our mental health to boosting our relationships with others. Explore ways you can be more appreciative in our mindful guide to gratitude. Read More ›.

Science suggests that expressing true gratitude boosts your health and spreads happiness. Here are a few simple exercises to help you build your capacity for gratitude. Read More ›.

In a recent development, gratitude isn’t just in our head: It takes root in our heart and in our senses, for one beautiful moment…and then the next. Here are three ways to practice gratitude, from a.m. to p.m. Read More ›.

Glenn Fox, PhD, is a research fellow at USC’s Brain and Creativity Institute. He earned his PhD from the Neuroscience Graduate Program at the University of Southern California working with Antonio Damasio. His research focuses on social cognition, affective neuroscience and social influence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

In a recent development, "Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:.

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits.

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

According to recent reports, vital: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

Sources indicate that this is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS claims "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 1: Calculate Combined Income.

Recent findings suggest that step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

In a recent development, step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:.

Industry observers note that sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:.

Industry observers note that the remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

Sources indicate that the FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

Recent findings suggest that this is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Sources indicate that every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:.

In a recent development, once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Sources indicate that delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

In a recent development, add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

Sources indicate that for the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

Industry observers note that the taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

Sources indicate that for single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

It has been revealed that no. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

Recent findings suggest that no — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

It has been revealed that social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

It has been revealed that there have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris. The work takes its name from a 13th-century Muslim shrine near Baalbek, northeast of Beirut, which is composed from the ruins of two separate ancient Roman sites: granite columns from Baalbek’s Temple of Jupiter hold up limestone sarcophagi from a necropolis.

Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.

Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.

It has been revealed that though Nasser is not the first artist to engage with Qubbat Duris, she points out, many of her antecedents are problematic. “The site has already been extensively imagined and reimagined in art historical painting,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “From Orientalist depictions to the backdrop to one of Gertrude Bell’s most circulated photographs, taken in costume on horseback.”.

Similar works of Nasser’s—such as Adonis River (2023) and Wedding at Qana (2024)—have also taken as their subjects “landscapes that loom large in historical painting but look nothing like the landscape itself in Western Asia, either overwhelmed by Orientalist tropes or painted as scenes of European countryside, betraying the artists’ lack of knowledge and limits of imagination”, she says. “I am trying to make paintings that are truthful to the landscape.”.

Recent findings suggest that the question of “truth” pertains to Qubbat Duris’s position as a site that reflects the layered cultural histories and religions of Lebanon. “It exists as a palimpsest from the second century AD until today, carrying all of the traces in between,” Nasser says.

Meanwhile, the role of evidence and recording in Nasser’s practice also considers the risks of erasure faced by much of Lebanon’s cultural artefacts, particularly from Israel’s longstanding and continued occupation of the country. On 15 October 2024, Qubbat Duris sustained slight damage from Israeli airstrikes; previously during the 2006 Israel-Lebanon war, an Israeli airstrike dislodged one of the shrine’s stones. “I’m interested in how a place like Qubbat Duris carries physical evidence of everything it’s endured, including scars of damage,” Nasser notes.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.
